gap.reason: The introduction identifies insufficient knowledge of how chemical complexity, size, and atomistic processes govern melting and premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.

source_text:
The synthesis of high entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs) has been conducted in the last year due to their outstanding behavior in catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion, and many other applications.1–4 The origin of their unique behavior is attributed to the chemical complexity introduced by the different atom types coexisting in the ordered crystalline structure.5–9 In particular, the design and functionalization of the NPs have been addressed as a route to improve the surface activation process in order to boost their application in different fields.10,11 The current demands in many fields have motivated understanding of the NPs’ physical and chemical responses under different scenarios.12

The novelty of HEA NPs arises from the different atomic sizes leading to modification of the electronic structure in terms of the atomic environment. Metallic HEA NPs of a few atoms showed that even the same component atoms display different local density of states that change in terms of the atomic neighborhood.5,13 Similar results have been conducted in body cubic centered TiZrHfNb HEA.14 The unique electronic structure has motivated several applications, such as an enhanced performance in hydrogen production on sub-20 Å NiCoFePtRh NPs, or superior electrocatalysis in alkaline oxygen reactions.15 Even more, nano–micro particles have been referred to as excellent materials for supercapacitors, or electrocatalyzer structures.15,16 The latter is motivated by the complex surfaces and chemical composition of HEA NPs, rendering different absorption energies which enable favorable adsorption to enhance the surface activity.

The previously mentioned applications have fueled the synthesis methods in the micro and nanoscale.17 To date, HEA nano and microparticles have been synthesized by means of different strategies such as carbothermal shock synthesis, fast moving bed pyrolysis, mechanical alloying, combinatorial sputtering, ultrasonic assisted wet chemistry, kinetically controlled laser synthesis, microwave assisted combustion synthesis, among many other methods.18–20 From all the mentioned synthesis strategies, at least five of them are based on thermal treatments that heat the precursors at high temperature to drive the element diffusion and mixing. The temperature cooling rate is also a fundamental factor that helps the consolidation of the solid solution before atomic diffusion could promote the segregation of the constituents.

The thermal response of NPs is currently addressed as a technique to understand how they will respond under more complex scenarios,21–23 and synthesis conditions.24–26 Besides, melting and premelting are crucial to delimit the NP applicability for diverse applications.27–29 Molecular dynamics simulations are typically introduced to unveil the atomistic mechanism that governs the phase transition on NPs of diverse morphology and composition.30–33 Samsonov et al.34 showed that the continuous melting in Ag and Au NPs is driven by means of a surface pre-melting mechanism. Al NPs with less than 1000 atoms have shown an interesting bi-stable behavior near to the melting point, which is attributed to the coexistence of a solid-to-liquid state at temperatures lower than the melting point.35 Pd NPs have shown very interesting behavior related to the NP shape, where cuboctahedron nanostructures display a melting from the NP corners. This is attributed to the surface stress as a consequence of the high facet indexes.36

Chemical complexity has been used as a tool to improve the performance of NPs. In this aspect, the coexistence of more than one element renders bimetallic NPs with different phases or complex morphology such as Core@Shell or Janus-like NPs. Au–Ag NPs have shown that alloying structures have a negative formation energy in comparison with Janus or Core@Shell nanostructures, demonstrating that for this kind of system the alloying is the more stable configuration.37 FeCu NPs have displayed a morphology dependence in terms of the atomic concentrations.38 By means of atomistic modeling, it was shown that the final configuration strongly depends on the surface energy of the respective Fe and Cu NPs. Although, in the current literature, many studies have been carried out on metallic NPs, studies on HEA NPs are still missing.39,40

It is worth mentioning that current experimental studies have achieved the synthesis of HEA nanostructures of diverse compositions.2 Even more recent studies have achieved the synthesis of HEA NPs with a hollow central cavity,41,42 which has been reported in the literature as a convenient morphology to boost the material performance in catalysis, sensing, energy storage, and many other applications.42 Size effects on melting point on HEA NPs were conducted through atomistic simulations on a system composed of PdPtRhCo atoms.39 Complementary studies have shown that there is no segregation on multiprincipal alloys.43 Other studies on AgAuPdPtNi HEAs have shown a size-dependent melting point typical of metallic NPs.39 Besides, some elements show a faster diffusion that could be relevant in the early stages of premelting of NPs.39,40 All in all, chemical complexity is a relevant factor that seems to influence thermal behavior in HEA NPs, however, theoretical understanding is still limited.

For this reason, this contribution is focused on the study of the melting of HEA NPs composed by FeNiCrCoCu atoms. Even more, possible size effects and atomistic understanding to unveil the fundamental physics processes that unleash the melting and premelting of HEA NPs will be discussed.

queries.broad: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles, what intervention could improve resistance to premature melting and thereby extend thermal applicability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its atomistic mechanism, predicts the change in premelting and melting behavior relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, defines the conditions under which the effect should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.
queries.problem_constrained: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles subjected to heating through the premelting and melting regime, what intervention could overcome susceptibility to thermally induced loss of structural stability? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts the premelting onset and melting response relative to untreated FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles, states the relevant particle-size and temperature boundaries, identifies supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and describes a falsification experiment.
queries.expert_context: Metallic-nanoparticle studies have reported surface-initiated premelting in Ag and Au, solid–liquid bistability below the melting point in Al particles containing fewer than 1000 atoms, and corner-initiated melting associated with surface stress in cuboctahedral Pd. Atomistic studies of PdPtRhCo and AgAuPdPtNi high-entropy nanoparticles found size-dependent melting, while some constituents exhibited faster diffusion during early premelting; other multiprincipal-alloy studies reported no segregation. Nevertheless, HEA-nanoparticle studies remain limited, particularly for FeNiCrCoCu, and thermal synthesis requires sufficient mixing and solid-solution consolidation before diffusion can promote constituent segregation. Under heating through premelting and melting, what intervention could improve the thermal stability of initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles while respecting these constraints? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its atomistic mechanism, the predicted response relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the particle-size and temperature conditions over which it should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that would falsify it.

queries.expert_context: Metallic-nanoparticle studies found surface premelting in Ag and Au and corner-origin melting in cuboctahedral Pd, attributed to surface stress from high-index facets. Experimental synthesis has produced high-entropy nanoparticles with diverse compositions, but their thermal behavior remains poorly understood. For initially crystalline nanoparticles composed of iron, nickel, chromium, cobalt, and copper under a temperature ramp spanning premelting and melting, what intervention could reduce thermally induced structural instability? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, explains its atomistic mechanism, predicts the response relative to an unchanged baseline, defines its applicability limits, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a decisive falsification experiment.

queries.broad: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion-related uses, and other applications requiring thermal stability, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing factor, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an outcome that would falsify it.
queries.problem_constrained: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.
queries.expert_context: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of both application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate a solid solution before constituent segregation can occur. Earlier studies found continuous melting in Ag and Au nanoparticles, bistability near melting in Al nanoparticles below 1000 atoms, and shape-dependent melting in Pd nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic nanoparticles also established composition- and morphology-dependent stable configurations. Studies of other high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles reported size-dependent melting points, an absence of segregation in some multiprincipal alloys, and unequal elemental diffusion during early premelting, but did not establish the governing physics for FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

queries.expert_context: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.
